transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for making time for this licensing review meeting. As you know, we're at the routine checkpoint before we send the HelioGrid outbound license package back to them. The current draft still has some significant gaps — we don't have a defined licensed field, a royalty rate, a minimum annual royalty, or any special compliance language. Before I approve this package to go out, I need final input from both of you. Patent counsel, I'd like your perspective on the field definition and any IP concerns. And commercial partnerships, I need your view on the commercial terms — royalty structure, exclusivity scope, and sublicensing flexibility. Let's start there.

transcript.text: Before we finalize this package, I need to flag something critical I found yesterday while reviewing the original federal grant file. The grant terms require that every license of the funded inventions must reserve government-use rights and include a U.S.-manufacturing plan before execution. I haven't circulated this analysis to the team yet, but this directly affects our HelioGrid license — the current draft has no special compliance language at all, and we'll need to address both the government-use rights reservation and a U.S.-manufacturing plan before this can go out, or we risk violating the grant terms.

transcript.text: I should share what I confirmed this morning. During our commercial review, the business sponsor made clear that our priority is to grant HelioGrid exclusive rights only in stationary grid-scale energy storage — electric-vehicle applications are expressly excluded. On pricing, the approved benchmark is a 6% royalty on net sales plus a $250,000 annual minimum. I haven't yet updated the draft instructions to reflect this, so the current draft still has those gaps Elena mentioned.
